title: The GUI Revolution — Xerox PARC, Mac, Windows

panels.prompt: The Xerox Alto computer from 1973, a boxy beige computer with a portrait-oriented screen showing windows and icons and a cursor, a three-button mouse sitting beside it on the desk, the screen glowing with a graphical interface, warm 1970s office setting, vintage and groundbreaking feeling, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, purple accent highlights Period-appropriate 1970s desk items only — papers, phone with rotary dial, NO modern technology, NO laptops.
panels.label: The Xerox Alto (1973) — windows, icons, menus, and a mouse

panels.text: Xerox PARC (Palo Alto Research Center), established in 1970, was building the future. By the mid-1970s, PARC had invented the graphical user interface, Ethernet, laser printing, WYSIWYG editing, and object-oriented programming. Their Alto (1973) integrated all of it — windows, icons, menus, and a mouse.

panels.prompt: A dramatic wide-shot scene in December 1979 at Xerox PARC, a young energetic man with dark hair in jeans and a black turtleneck, arms raised excitedly, face electrified with inspiration, while a researcher in glasses demonstrates a graphical interface on an Alto computer screen nearby, other researchers watching with mixed expressions, tension and excitement in the air, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, purple and amber lighting
panels.label: Steve Jobs at Xerox PARC, December 1979 — 'Why aren't you DOING anything with this?!'

panels.text: In December 1979, Steve Jobs visited PARC. Researcher Larry Tesler demonstrated the Alto. Jobs was electrified: "Why aren't you doing anything with this? This is the greatest thing! This is revolutionary!" Not everyone agreed — Adele Goldberg, a key developer of Smalltalk, objected to giving away PARC's crown jewels. She was overruled by management.

panels.label: Windows 1.0, November 1985 — slow, limited, but the beginning

panels.text: The Apple Macintosh launched January 24, 1984 at $2,495, with the legendary "1984" commercial by Ridley Scott. Apple didn't just copy PARC — they added the menu bar, drag-and-drop, and a simplified single-button mouse. Microsoft followed with Windows 1.0 in November 1985 — clunky and limited. It wasn't until Windows 3.0 (1990) that their GUI succeeded commercially.

panels.caption: The GUI lineage — no single entity invented the graphical interface

panels.text: The GUI did not make computers more powerful. It made computers more accessible. And accessibility is a kind of power — the power to bring millions of new minds into the computing revolution.

Think About It: Every interface is a tradeoff. Command lines are fast and precise for experts. GUIs are intuitive for everyone. Today we are asking the same question again: is talking to an AI assistant the next interface revolution? What will that make possible?

panels.text: Step back and look at where we are. In just two decades, software became portable. Computers became personal. Networks began connecting them. Interfaces became visual. And a movement declared that software should be free. But there is one enormous problem still unsolved...
